newsitem.title: CHINA: Russia calls for troop cut in Korean peninsula.
newsitem.headline: Russia calls for troop cut in Korean peninsula.

text.p: Russian defence minister Igor Rodionov has called for a reduction in troops on the Korean peninsula, warning that the United States, Russia and China would be dragged in to any conflict that broke out there.

"We believe that it is important to create measures of trust in the military field, such as radical reductions of troops and weapons in the (Korean) peninsula, including those of the United States," Rodionov said in a speech in Beijing on Tuesday.

His remarks came just days before President Jiang Zemin is to visit Moscow to sign an accord with Russia's President Boris Yeltsin and leaders of the Central Asian states of Tajikistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan on cutting military forces along the former Soviet-Chinese border.

Rodionov, who arrived in China on Sunday for a five-day visit, did not say when or by how much he thought the troops in the Korean peninsula should be cut, said a Russian source who had a copy of his speech to the Academy of Military Sciences.
South Korea has 690,000 troops against North Korea's 1,055,000 troops. There are 36,450 U.S. troops in South Korea.
U.S. troops should be replaced with a force from neutral countries in the Korean Demilitarized Zone, Rodionov said.
The United States and China would be sucked in if conflict broke out on the Korean peninsula, he warned, adding that Russia would not sit idle in the event of a conflict.
Rodionov defended Russia's arms sales to China, saying weapons sold were defensive in nature and would not alter the balance of power in the Asia-Pacific region.
The arms sales were not aimed at a third country, he said.
Russia is China's biggest arms supplier. China has acquired Sukhoi 27 fighters from Russia and was building fighters at home under licence from Russia.
China is eager to buy more SU-27 fighters as well as two Sovremenny guided-missile destroyers and Kilo-class submarines from Russia, military analysts have said.
Rodionov said Russia opposed Western countries using issues such as human rights, Tibet or Taiwan to interfere in China's internal affairs.
China on Tuesday sank a U.N. resolution in Geneva to censure its human rights record. Russia abstained, effectively blocking scrutiny of China's human rights record.

During his visit, Rodionov has held talks with his Chinese counterpart, Chi Haotian, met Liu Huaqing, vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, and underlined the importance of what the two neighbours call their strategic alliance.
He was expected to meet China's Communist Party chief and state president Jiang and to visit the northeastern naval base of Fushun, once a Russian treaty port called Port Arthur.
Rodionov's visit is the latest sign of warming relations between the two countries, coming just before Jiang's planned visit to Moscow, scheduled for April 22-26.

Jiang's trip is aimed at building closer ties after decades of distrust and would promote Russia's aim of better relations in the East when it faces difficulties in relations with the West over NATO's plans to expand eastwards.
China and Russia formed a strong alliance in the early 1950s but it degenerated into bitter rivalry for leadership of the communist world and border clashes in the late 1960s.

Relations have been warming since Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev visited Beijing in 1989. Visits to China by Yeltsin in December 1992 and in April last year maintained the improvement in ties and Jiang said last year that relations with Russia had entered a new age.
